name: Mnemba Atoll Snorkelling
summary: A dhow out to the reef on the atoll's western shelf, with two snorkelling stops and fruit on the boat.
description: The boat leaves from the beach in front of the village and takes about forty minutes to reach the shelf, where the reef sits in three to eight metres of very clear water. Two stops of roughly forty-five minutes each, with a break between them for fruit and water. Turtles are common on the northern stop and are not fed or handled. The atoll itself is a private island; the snorkelling is in the conservation area around it, and landing is not permitted.
meeting_point_text: Nungwi main beach, by the blue dhow shelter north of the fish market

name: Spice Farm Tour
summary: A working farm north of town: cloves, nutmeg, cinnamon and vanilla, picked and passed round rather than pointed at.
description: Zanzibar's spice trade is the reason Stone Town looks the way it does, and this is the short version told on the ground. A guide walks you through a smallholding at Kizimbani, cutting bark and crushing leaves as you go, and the tasting at the end is of whatever is ripe rather than a fixed list. Lunch is Zanzibari, cooked at the farm, and is included.
meeting_point_text: Darajani Market main entrance, opposite the fish hall

name: Prison Island Half Day
summary: Changuu Island by boat: the giant tortoises, the quarantine ruins, and an hour on the sandbank.
description: Changuu was bought to hold enslaved people, then used as a quarantine station, and now holds a colony of Aldabra giant tortoises given by the Seychelles in the 1919. The boat is twenty minutes each way from Forodhani, and the visit is an hour with the tortoises, a walk round the ruins, and time to swim off the western beach.
meeting_point_text: Forodhani Gardens jetty, in front of the Old Dispensary

name: Stone Town Walking Tour
summary: Three hours on foot through the old town, ending at the seafront in time for the night market.
description: The House of Wonders, the Old Fort, the former slave market and the cathedral built over it, the Anglican mission, and the doors — which are the reason people photograph this town and the thing most visitors never get explained. The route is deliberately narrow-street-heavy and does not use a vehicle at any point.
meeting_point_text: The Old Fort courtyard, by the amphitheatre steps

name: Kitesurfing Beginner Lesson
summary: Three hours on the lagoon at Paje, one instructor to two students, kit included.
description: Paje's lagoon is flat, waist-deep for several hundred metres at low tide, and steadily windy from June to September and December to March — which is why it is the place people learn. The session covers kite setup, the wind window, body dragging and a first attempt at the board. Two students per instructor, and no previous experience is assumed.
meeting_point_text: Paje beach, the kite school container north of the main beach bar

name: Jozani Forest and Red Colobus
summary: The last of the island's groundwater forest, its endemic monkeys, and the mangrove boardwalk.
description: The Zanzibar red colobus lives nowhere else and there are perhaps two and a half thousand of them, most within a few kilometres of this forest. The troop nearest the road is habituated and is watched from a set distance the guides enforce. The mangrove boardwalk afterwards is a kilometre through standing water and is the part most people remember.
meeting_point_text: Jozani-Chwaka Bay National Park visitor centre car park

name: Sunset Dhow Cruise
summary: Two hours on a rigged dhow off the north-west coast, timed to put the sun behind the sail.
description: A traditional dhow with a lateen sail, crewed by two, leaving ninety minutes before sunset from Nungwi beach. The boat sails north-west far enough to clear the headland and then holds position off Kendwa. Fruit, samosas and a soft drink are served on board. It does not become a party boat and there is no music.
meeting_point_text: Nungwi main beach, opposite the Baraka Aquarium turning

name: Mnemba Two-Tank Dive
summary: Two dives on the Mnemba wall for certified divers, with a surface interval on the boat.
description: The wall on the eastern side of the atoll runs from twelve to about thirty metres and has reliable visibility outside the rainy months. Two dives with a full surface interval between them, on a boat that takes eight divers and carries oxygen and a first-aid kit. A current certification card is checked at the shop before boarding, and a refresher is not part of this trip.
meeting_point_text: Matemwe dive centre, on the beach path behind the village mosque

name: Kiwengwa Caves and Village Walk
summary: The coral caves behind the village, and the walk back through the seaweed farms.
description: The caves are limestone, still used for ceremonies, and the guide is from the village rather than from a tour company. The walk back goes past the seaweed plots the women here farm on the low tide, which is the main income in this stretch of coast and is explained at some length because it is worth it.
meeting_point_text: Kiwengwa village square, by the primary school gate

name: Sandbank Picnic
summary: A boat out to a bank that is only there for four hours, with lunch cooked on it.
description: The bank sits off Kendwa and appears on the falling tide. The boat drops you with a shade sail, a cool box and a cook, and lunch is grilled on the sand. It is worth understanding that the timing follows the tide rather than the clock, so the departure moves through the week and the return is not negotiable.
meeting_point_text: Kendwa beach, at the north end by the boat mooring poles

name: Michamvi Sunset Kayak
summary: Two hours in a sit-on-top along the mangrove edge of Chwaka Bay, on the only west-facing beach on the east coast.
description: Michamvi Kae faces west, which is why the sunsets here are the ones people come round the peninsula for. The paddle is inside the bay, sheltered, and follows the mangrove line before crossing to the beach. Doubles are available and no experience is needed.
meeting_point_text: Michamvi Kae beach, by the kayak rack at the south end

name: Safari Blue Full Day
summary: A full day out of Fumba: sandbanks, snorkelling, a mangrove lagoon and a seafood lunch on Kwale.
description: The original of the format, run out of Fumba on the south-west peninsula since the 1990s. A dhow takes you out through the Menai Bay conservation area, stopping to snorkel, then to the lagoon behind Kwale island, and finally to the island itself for a grilled lunch and the fruit tasting the trip is known for. Dolphins are often seen in the bay and are never chased.
meeting_point_text: Fumba fishing village jetty, at the Safari Blue office
